CA-02.001: atoms have a compact nucleus surrounded by electrons. the number of protons in the nucleus defines the element. a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. changing the number of electrons changes its electric charge, giving an ion. atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. these forms are isotopes. for example, carbon-12 and carbon-13 each have six protons. they have six and seven neutrons, respectively. atomic images depend on how an instrument interacts with a specimen and displays the result. a drawing with fixed electron tracks is also a simplified representation. isotope ion
CA-02.002: energy measures the state and changes of physical systems. a falling object gives an example. in a model with negligible air resistance, the gravitational potential energy of the object–earth system decreases while the object's kinetic energy increases. energy can transfer between systems. an object sliding to a stop on a rough surface warms the object and the surface, as some organized motion becomes internal energy. in an isolated system the total energy is conserved even as the form or location of the energy changes. the accounting depends on which objects and interactions are included in the system. the falling-object example uses an everyday mechanical approximation. kinetic energy isolated system
CA-02.003: atoms can form molecules. in a covalent bond, a pair of atoms shares electrons. a water molecule consists of an oxygen atom covalently bonded to two hydrogen atoms. the atoms form a bent arrangement. chemical behavior depends on composition and arrangement. for example, carbon dioxide is linear and water is bent. combined with differences in how different atoms attract shared electrons, geometry affects the distribution of electric charge and how a molecule interacts with its surroundings. a ball-and-stick drawing is a geometrical model. the sticks and size of the spheres do not depict the detailed distribution of electrons. molecule covalent bond
CA-02.004: a star such as the sun emits energy sustained for much of its life by fusion. the solar system contains the sun and the objects bound to it by gravity, including planets, smaller orbiting bodies and their moons. earth follows an orbit around the sun. the sun is one of the many stars in the milky way. a galaxy is a larger gravitational system with stars, gas, dust and other matter. images of the solar system and a distant galaxy show different scales and kinds of structure. the solar system montage assembles separate pictures. astronomical maps and composites may combine different instruments or times. read the provenance and scale before comparing apparent sizes on the page. solar system galaxy
CA-02.005: the sun and its planetary system developed from material in a cloud of gas and dust. gravity drew material together. a rotating disk surrounded the growing star. in the disk, small solid particles grew into larger bodies through accumulation and some collisions. meteorites preserve material from the early solar system. observations of disks around young stars provide another way to investigate how planetary systems form. planet formation concerns the assembly of a planetary body. the emergence of living systems is a separate question. this is a simplified formation model; the detailed history of individual bodies remains under investigation. accretion meteorite
CA-02.006: electromagnetic radiation can carry energy through empty space. a wave description uses wavelength, the distance between equivalent points such as adjacent crests, and frequency, the number of cycles per unit time. in a vacuum, wavelength multiplied by frequency gives the speed of light. radio waves have longer wavelengths than the radiation human eyes normally detect. an instrument can measure intensity in a range of wavelengths and assign colors to display those measurements. the result can show structures invisible to unaided eyes. the display colors then belong to the visualization convention and need the instrument's legend to interpret. a wave description is sufficient for these examples. some measurements require describing transfers of energy in discrete quanta. wavelength spectrum
CA-02.007: stars form when gravity gathers gas within clouds. if the center becomes sufficiently hot and dense, nuclei can fuse there. for much of the sun's lifetime, fusion converts hydrogen to helium in the core. energy transported to the surface escapes as radiation. mass influences how a star develops. a star like the sun can expand into a red giant and eventually leave a compact white dwarf. some much more massive stars undergo core collapse. some such collapses produce a supernova, and a neutron star or black hole can remain. these are illustrative paths for single stars. rotation, chemical composition and interactions with companion stars can change events and outcomes. nuclear fusion white dwarf
CA-02.008: when two objects at different temperatures make thermal contact, energy tends to move from the warmer object to the cooler one. this transfer due to a temperature difference is called heat. a temperature describes the thermal condition of a system. a large and a small volume of the same liquid can share a temperature while containing different amounts of internal energy. a phase is a form of matter with uniform physical properties. ice and liquid water are different phases that can coexist during melting. whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas can depend on both temperature and pressure. boiling begins when the vapor pressure of the liquid reaches the surrounding pressure. these examples describe familiar materials close to thermal equilibrium. temperature alone cannot determine the phase without additional conditions. heat vapor pressure
CA-02.009: gravity changes the motion of objects. in newton's model, two point masses attract each other. for the same masses, doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter. outside nearly spherical bodies the model uses distance between their centers. an orbit can be understood as continuing free fall. a spacecraft moving sideways falls toward earth while its path curves around the planet. if one body is much more massive, many bound paths are approximated by an ellipse with that mass at one focus. the period is the time for one circuit of a repeating orbit. these examples use a newtonian model with simplified bodies. gravity from other bodies, drag, propulsion and relativistic effects can matter in more precise calculations. orbit orbital period
CA-02.010: a spectrometer separates radiation by wavelength and measures how much arrives in different bands. a hot dense object can give a broad spectrum. a dilute excited gas can emit strongly at particular wavelengths, appearing as bright lines in a graph or image. when broad-spectrum light passes through a cooler gas, some wavelengths can be absorbed more strongly, appearing as dark lines. comparing observed patterns with laboratory spectra helps identify atoms or molecules along the path. a spectrum of a star therefore gives evidence beyond the color seen by an eye. multiple substances and physical conditions can contribute to the same observation. motion can shift wavelengths and finite instrument resolution can blend lines. a single line may not identify its source. spectrometer spectral line
CA-02.011: in an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into different combinations. existing bonds can change or break, and new bonds can form. reactants are the substances taking part at the start. products are substances formed by the reaction. a chemical equation can count the atoms before and after a reaction. two hydrogen molecules have four hydrogen atoms in total. one oxygen molecule has two oxygen atoms. together they account for the atoms in two water molecules. a balanced equation conserves the number of atoms of each element. the counts in a balanced equation do not specify when a reaction will occur or how fast. the example describes atom accounting without forming a laboratory procedure. reactant product
